INTRODUCTION
Turner (1895) described and mapped a patchwork of distinctive
Tertiary basalt outcrops in the northern Sierra NevadaMountainsthat
extends 100 km from northeast to southwest. Durrell (1959) named
thesebasaltstheLovejoyFormationandarguedthattheyaretherem-
nants of a series of great flows that crossed the Sierra Nevada in an
ancestral river valley, where they flooded into lowlands that are now
the Sacramento Valley and spread at least 70 km farther tothenorth-
westand130kmtothesouthwest.Wagneretal.(2000)suggestedthat
the Lovejoy basalt flows were part of the same 17–14 Maoutpouring
of lava flows, attributed to the Yellowstone hotspot, that compose the
voluminous Columbia River flood basalt and high plateau lavas of
Washington, Oregon, and western Idaho (Fig. 1). If this hypothesis is
correct, it greatly extends the southwestward extent of Yellowstone
hotspot volcanism.
Asrecentlyas10yragostratigraphicinterpretationsregardingthe
Lovejoy Formation were hotly disputed and K-Ar dates were highly
variable. Estimates for the age of various outcrops ranged from late
Eocene to early Pliocene. Now five 40Ar/39Arstep-heatingdetermina-
tions areavailablethatclusterbetween15.5and16.4Ma(Pageetal.,
1995; Garrison, 2004). The Lovejoy flows are remarkably homoge-
neous geochemically and much more similar to Grande Ronde flows
of the Columbia River Basalt (though significantly higher in Ba, K,
and P) than to other basalt flows in the less distant Sierra Nevada,
Coast Range, and Cascade Arc (Siegel, 1988; Garrison, 2004). Geo-
chemicalfingerprintingofindividualunitsisdifficult,andmegascopic Figure1.A:WesternUnitedStatesshowinglocationofLovejoyBa-
and microscopic properties are generally inadequate for this purpose salt (LJB) relativeto ColumbiaRiverBasalt(CRB),OregonPlateau
